notes: Independent Round-2 verifier answers. Only reviews/blind/G.json consulted. G-COSTMODEL-020 answered independently before consulting the repair record.

answers.rationale: Ansor's central design intent: algorithmic sketches over multi-op subgraphs, learned cost model for pruning, prioritize subgraphs by end-to-end contribution — removes per-op manual templates while keeping search tractable.

Both C1 and C2 measure 0.42 ± 0.03 ms; the gap (0.02–0.03 ms) is within one noise std. Winner-take-all is dominated by variance. Fix: more repetitions per trial, robust statistic (median-of-medians) or equivalence band.

A: one-off runs don't amortize compile. B: recompile on shape change inflates effective budget. D: long-lived services easily amortize hours. C false — tuning affects the artifact & recompile latency for serving.
Constant fold (mul 2,3 → 6), CSE (%t3, %t4 both add %x, %c6 → one), DCE (%unused). All three are classical semantics-preserving optimizations; returning the same SSA value twice is valid.
A false — analytical models diverge from measurement in principle. B: spills predicted post-lowering. C: cache/TLB variability from environment. D: warmup effects like JIT/lazy load/clock ramp.

Vertical = merge producer/consumer along data-flow edge; horizontal = merge independent ops sharing input or launch dims; epilogue = attach lightweight elementwise to tail of heavy compute (GEMM+bias+GELU).

Fusion into reduction is semantically legal, but if T must remain materialized for consumer Z (of T), the fused kernel re-executes f inside reduction while Z still reads original T — compiler must duplicate compute or forgo fusion.

A: cross-device requires explicit copy. B: mutation with aliased live consumer violates side-effect ordering. C: iteration-space rank mismatch — need a common loop-nest. D: graph-output tensors must be materialized. E false (register pressure isn't unbounded), F false (pointwise-pointwise same-shape is exactly what fusion targets).
GEMM epilogue must expose a slot that applies pointwise chain in registers before storing tiles; otherwise pointwise ops read/write the full M×N via DRAM and traffic is unchanged. A/C/D wrong.

Fused kernel: live-range union → 96 regs/thread → 48 B spills, occupancy 25%. Spill-driven local-memory traffic exceeds DRAM traffic saved by removing the intermediate. Classic register-pressure fusion regression.

Halide's key insight: one algorithm admits many valid schedules with vastly different perf; separating them lets programmer/autoscheduler explore schedules without touching correctness-critical algorithm, enabling portability across CPU/GPU/DSP by re-scheduling.

Log explicitly states 'fusing would force reduction to broadcast pointwise input, producing >2× the memory traffic' — this is a fusion-cost heuristic based on estimated added memory traffic. B/C/D overstate absolutes.

Kernel selection = for each op instance choose concrete impl (library call / generated kernel / fused template) based on op-type, shape, dtype, layout, target hw — optionally with cost-model or measurement ranking.

NHWC makes channel the fastest-varying axis, matching Tensor Core / im2col-tile access patterns; NCHW places channel as strided outer axis which Tensor Core NHWC kernels don't support directly, so cuDNN picks a different (lower-utilization) algorithm.

B: fission relieves register pressure. C: fission separates vectorizable from non-vectorizable statements. D: different tile sizes for compute-bound vs memory-bound halves. A describes when fission is BAD (already fits & reuse within iter), not a motivation for it.

In the fused loop, iteration i reads B[i+1] which hasn't been produced yet (that happens in iteration i+1). This violates the flow (RAW) dependence from producer to consumer, so the fusion is illegal without additional transformations (e.g., shifting).

Memory planning: compiler analyzes tensor lifetimes globally, groups non-overlapping lifetimes into shared storage, produces static allocation plan executed without per-op malloc/free — distinct from runtime allocator caching.

A: manual templates don't generalize. B: learned cost model captures spills/bank conflicts better than analytical. C: sketch abstraction structures the search space. D false — real measurement remains essential (cost models are proxies). E false — auto search often matches or beats manual templates given enough budget.

A: reductions need assoc/commut or explicit reduction clause. C: no output dependence. D: no true / anti dependence across iterations. B false — branches don't per se prevent parallelization; only cross-iteration dependences do.

A: fair baseline is vendor-tuned per target. C: comparable per-target tuning required. D: portability = ability to generate good schedules across targets, not a single artifact. B false — TC utilization % ignores different algorithms/dtypes.

A: recompute wins when memory savings enable larger batch/seq gains. B: cheap op with large activation is favorable. E: selective by memory-per-FLOP ratio wins. C false (compute-bound + small activation = bad candidate). D false (recomputation is bitwise-equivalent if deterministic).

ikj: inner loop over j reads B[k,:] and writes C[i,:] with unit stride on row-major; A[i,k] is loop-invariant in the inner loop. Same +='s → semantically equivalent, better locality than ijk (which strides through B by N).

Template-based (AutoTVM): developer writes template with parameter placeholders; search explores parameters of fixed template. Template-free (Ansor/MetaSchedule): candidates auto-generated by combining schedule primitives — no template needed, larger space.

A: constant-dependent unrolls/tile sizes need known dims. B: dynamic-shape trades per-shape perf for compile-time & storage economy. E: bucketing hybrids capture much of speed while bounding cache. C false (per-shape compile & dispatch time hurt one-off shapes). D false — dynamic-shape compilers handle shape-dependent numerics correctly.
3 × 64² × 4 = 3 × 4096 × 4 = 49,152 B = 48 KB exactly. Options A/B/C either overflow or under-utilize.

At M=N=K=1024 with 128×128 tile → only 8 grid blocks; A100 has 108 SMs, so ~92% of SMs idle. Smaller 64×64 tile → 256 blocks fill all SMs. Root cause: insufficient parallelism / grid tail effect, not tile arithmetic intensity.
Cost model transfers when features (op class, dtype, hw) are similar. Different op class (GEMM→Conv) or hardware (A100→H100) shifts the feature distribution, negating transfer benefit.

B: split is legality-free (relabel). C: reorder requires dependence-preserving order. D: vectorize requires independent iterations + compatible trip count. A false — bind requires legality for GPU thread mapping; cross-iteration writes into shared state are not automatically handled.
Unroll 8× on already-tight loop can triple object-code size, evict hot code from L1I, materially slowing the function. Loop-overhead savings are outweighed by I-cache/decoder pressure. A/B/C false.

Reads A[i-1] and A[i] — both READS, no cross-iteration write, so vectorization is legal. Compiler needs: (i) unaligned/shifted load for A[i-1] and (ii) tail handling when N mod 8 != 0. C false (only reads, no write dependence).
